items.title: Brijesh Nanda B Y Receives Best Poster Award at AgWireless’26
items.description: Brijesh Nanda B Y received the Best Poster Award at AgWireless’26 for No-Code Workflow Studio, an ICICLE-enabled platform that makes agricultural automation accessible through a visual, no-code interface.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
The Systems and AI (SAI) Lab is pleased to announce that Brijesh Nanda B Y received the Best Poster Award at AgWireless’26 for his poster, “No-Code Workflow Studio.”

The recognition highlights work developed under the umbrella of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute to make advanced automation technologies more accessible to agricultural users. The No-Code Workflow Studio enables users to design and deploy automation workflows through a visual interface, reducing the need for specialized programming expertise.

At AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show, Brijesh demonstrated the platform through a precision zone-spraying workflow. The demonstration illustrated how a user could configure a data-informed agricultural workflow for a practical field operation without writing code.

The SAI Lab congratulates Brijesh on this achievement and looks forward to continuing its work on practical, trustworthy, and accessible AI systems for agriculture.

items.title: SAI Lab Showcases ICICLE-Enabled Agricultural AI at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show
items.description: SAI Lab Showcases ICICLE-Enabled Agricultural AI at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show; Brijesh Nanda B Y receives Best Poster Award for the No-Code Workflow Studio; the SAI Lab team engages farmers, researchers, and industry partners on practical AI and edge-computing challenges in agriculture.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
The Systems and AI (SAI) Lab recently participated in AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show, bringing research demonstrations in artificial intelligence, workflow automation, and edge computing to a community of agricultural producers, technology developers, researchers, and industry leaders.

The events provided a valuable opportunity to present technologies developed under the umbrella of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and to engage directly with the people and organizations working to advance connected, data-driven agriculture. AgWireless’26 combined an ARA User Program, an NSF workshop on rural-focused NextG and agricultural innovation, and demonstrations at the Farm Progress Show; the ICICLE AI Institute was among the featured exhibitors.

Demonstrating practical agricultural AI

At the events, the SAI Lab presented two complementary technologies intended to make advanced computing capabilities more usable in agricultural environments.

No-Code Workflow Studio

Led by Brijesh Nanda B Y, the No-Code Workflow Studio enables users to design and deploy automation workflows without writing software code. The team demonstrated a precision zone-spraying workflow to show how agricultural users could configure an automated, data-informed process for a field-level application.

The work addresses a recurring barrier in the adoption of advanced agricultural technology: powerful tools often require specialized programming or systems expertise. By providing a no-code interface, the platform is designed to help domain users focus on defining their operational workflow rather than implementing its underlying software components.

Intelligent Edge Management Service

Led by Harikesh Byrandurga Gopinath, the Intelligent Edge Management Service focuses on managing edge devices and data in distributed settings. Agricultural deployments often involve heterogeneous sensors, cameras, machines, networks, and computing resources that operate far from centralized data centers. Effective management of these resources is essential for dependable field data collection, communication, and timely AI-enabled analysis.

Together, the No-Code Workflow Studio and Intelligent Edge Management Service represent complementary parts of a broader agricultural intelligence pipeline: making it easier to specify automation and supporting the reliable edge infrastructure needed to execute it.

Best Poster recognition

A highlight of the week was the recognition of Brijesh Nanda B Y’s poster, “No-Code Workflow Studio,” with the Best Poster Award.

The award recognizes the technical contribution and its potential relevance to accessible agricultural automation. It also reflects the importance of designing AI and cyberinfrastructure tools that can be used by a broad range of stakeholders—not only specialists with extensive software-development experience. AgWireless’26 included a formal poster and demo session with Best Poster and Honorable Mention awards.

Learning through collaboration

Beyond demonstrations and presentations, the SAI Lab used the events to learn from agricultural stakeholders and explore future collaborative opportunities.

Conversations with farmers, researchers, and industry participants centered on practical challenges that continue to shape the future of agricultural technology: reliable rural connectivity, integration across diverse edge devices, usable interfaces, scalable data management, and the translation of AI prototypes into systems that can support real operational decisions.

The team also participated in the ARA User Program and Arathon, which brought participants together for hands-on engagement with ARA systems and data. The experience supported the lab’s ongoing exploration of how ARA infrastructure and agricultural data may inform future digital-twin and edge-AI research directions. The ARA User Program and Arathon were core components of AgWireless’26.

Early discussions with organizations including Raptor Dynamics and Airstrike Ag also opened channels for potential future exchange and collaboration. These conversations remain exploratory, but they provide useful insight into areas of shared interest across the AgTech ecosystem.

Moving from research to impact

The SAI Lab’s participation at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show reflects a broader commitment to developing AI systems that are not only technically advanced, but also practical, accessible, and responsive to real-world conditions.

items.title: SAI Lab at PEARC 2026
items.description: SAI Lab members participated in PEARC 2026 through tutorials, Birds of a Feather sessions, and demos of ICICLE tools including Smart Labeler, Preprocessing Studio, and Edge Device Manager.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
Members of the SAI Lab participated in PEARC 2026, engaging with the research computing community through tutorials, Birds of a Feather sessions, live demonstrations, and informal conversations with peers from across the field. The event provided an excellent opportunity to showcase our work in AI-enabled cyberinfrastructure and to learn from others building tools for scalable scientific computing.

A hands-on tutorial with collaborators from TACC and ICICLE highlighted several services developed to support machine learning and data-centric research. Attendees explored various ICICLE tools including the Smart Labeler developed by members of SAI Lab for streamlining data annotation workflows. The interactive format encouraged discussion about usability, integration, and how these services can fit into larger research pipelines.

The SAI Lab also contributed to poster and demo sessions featuring the broader ICICLE service ecosystem. These demonstrations showed how tools developed by SAI Lab for ICICLE such as Smart Labeler, No-Code Image Lab (Preprocessing Studio), and Edge Device Manager can work together to support end-to-end AI workflows, from data preparation to deployment on edge devices. Conversations with attendees reinforced the importance of building systems that are not only technically capable, but also practical and accessible for real-world use.

Another key theme was workflow orchestration. We shared our vision for a pluggable Workflow Orchestrator that can adapt to different research tasks by swapping stages in and out as needed. We also previewed upcoming capabilities, including shapefile generation, which will help generate mission files for drone systems when onboard compute is not available.

Beyond our own sessions, the Nexus presentation offered useful ideas around cross-cluster data synchronization, synced local development environments, streamlined GPU access, and temporary SSH credential management. These concepts were especially relevant as we continue building cyberinfrastructure that supports flexible, reproducible, and scalable AI research.

PEARC 2026 was a valuable opportunity for the SAI Lab to share our work, connect with the broader community, and gather ideas that will inform the next generation of our tools and services.

items.title: Bringing AI to the Field: ICICLE and SAI Lab Showcase Scalable Agricultural Intelligence at the 2026 Ohio State Fair
items.description: SAI Lab / ICICLE presented Auto-Harvest, Intelligent Edge Management Service (IEMS), and Smart Labeler at the 2026 Ohio State Fair, demonstrating end-to-end AI and cyberinfrastructure for precision agriculture.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
The members of SAI Lab / ICICLE had an exceptional opportunity to present ICICLE’s AI-driven cyberinfrastructure at the 2026 Ohio State Fair, demonstrating how advanced computing and intelligent systems are reshaping the future of precision agriculture. Through live, interactive demonstrations, our team from the SAI Lab engaged a wide audience—ranging from farmers and students to industry leaders—bridging cutting-edge research with practical, field-ready solutions.

At the core of our showcase were three complementary innovations that together enable an end-to-end agricultural intelligence pipeline. First, our Auto-Harvest framework demonstrated how autonomous UAV-based image acquisition integrates with high-performance computing (HPC) pipelines to support timely and precise field interventions. Attendees were particularly interested in how this pipeline reduces manual scouting efforts while enabling data-driven decision-making at scale.

Second, we presented the Intelligent Edge Management Service (IEMS), developed within the NSF ICICLE AI Institute. IEMS enables seamless orchestration of containerized AI workloads and real-time inference directly on edge devices, even in rural environments with limited connectivity. This capability resonated strongly with participants interested in deploying AI systems beyond traditional cloud settings, highlighting the importance of low-latency, resilient edge-to-cloud architectures.

Third, our Smart Labeler platform addressed a critical bottleneck in AI adoption: data annotation. By leveraging HPC resources, Smart Labeler supports rapid, scalable, multi-modal dataset labeling across domains, significantly accelerating the development and deployment of AI models.

Beyond the technical demonstrations, the event provided a valuable platform for dialogue and collaboration. We engaged in meaningful conversations with agricultural practitioners, technology developers, and business leaders exploring how ICICLE’s AI and cyberinfrastructure ecosystem can be integrated into real-world operations. These exchanges underscored a growing demand for scalable, accessible AI solutions that can operate reliably in field conditions.

The accompanying images capture these interactions—our students and staff demonstrating live systems, walking attendees through workflows, and discussing practical deployment scenarios. These moments highlight not only the technical capabilities of our platforms but also their accessibility and relevance to diverse user communities.

Overall, the Ohio State Fair served as a powerful venue to translate research into impact. The enthusiasm and curiosity we encountered reaffirm the importance of bringing advanced AI and cyberinfrastructure innovations directly to the public, fostering both awareness and adoption in domains critical to societal and economic sustainability.

items.title: SAI Lab Undergraduates Advance to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0
items.description: Ohio State undergraduates Amrithaa Ashok Kumar, Aarush Katta, and Maanav Jajodia advanced to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0 in the Remote Sensing and Yield Prediction track.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Ohio State undergraduates Amrithaa Ashok Kumar, Aarush Katta, and Maanav Jajodia, who are affiliated with the Systems and AI Lab (SAI Lab) at The Ohio State University and the NSF ICICLE AI Institute, have advanced to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0, an international AI for Science and Engineering hackathon organized by the Anusandhan National Research Foundation in collaboration with IIIT Hyderabad, GalaxEye, and IIT Madras.

Their team is competing in the Remote Sensing and Yield Prediction track, which challenges participants to develop robust AI methods for crop-pattern detection and yield prediction using remote sensing and geospatial data.

In Round 1, the team developed a crop-mapping pipeline that integrates multi-temporal X-band synthetic aperture radar imagery, agricultural masking, temporal feature extraction, and unsupervised machine learning to estimate village-level crop areas in settings with sparse and limited ground-truth data.

This work reflects the SAI Lab's broader interests in AI, cyberinfrastructure, and data-driven agriculture, while also aligning closely with ICICLE's use-inspired emphasis on digital agriculture.

AISEHack 2.0 brings together students, researchers, innovators, and AI practitioners to address real-world scientific and engineering challenges, with shortlisted teams moving on to a second online sprint and top finalists advancing to the Grand Finale in Goa, India.

items.title: AI-Driven Conservation Decision Framework Presented at ICPA 2026
items.description: Research led by Khushboo Mundada on an AI-driven decision framework connecting conservation practices, climate conditions, crop yield, and conservation payments was presented at the 17th International Conference on Precision Agriculture in Porto Alegre, Brazil.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
Research developed by Khushboo Mundada was presented at the 17th International Conference on Precision Agriculture (ICPA), held jointly with the 11th Brazilian Congress on Precision and Digital Agriculture (ConBAP) from July 13–16, 2026, in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

Presented by Dr. John Fulton, the work introduced an AI-driven decision framework designed to connect agricultural conservation practices, climate conditions, crop-yield outcomes, and conservation-payment decisions. The research was based on Khushboo's thesis work and focused on transforming multiple environmental and management indicators into an interpretable decision matrix that can support agricultural planning and conservation-program evaluation.

A key component of the framework is the use of probabilistic yield prediction. Instead of producing only a single estimated yield value, the model represents a range of possible outcomes and their associated probabilities. The quality of these predictions is evaluated using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), which compares the complete predicted probability distribution with the actual observed yield. A lower CRPS indicates that the predicted distribution is more accurate and better aligned with the observed outcome.

The framework also incorporates the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index over a 12-month period, known as SPEI-12. This indicator measures whether an area has experienced relatively wet, normal, or dry conditions by considering both precipitation and water loss through evapotranspiration. SPEI-12 allows the model to account for longer-term moisture conditions that may influence crop performance and the effectiveness of conservation practices.

Another major element is the Conservation Effectiveness Score (CES), which represents a farm's recent conservation-management history. The score combines five years of conservation practices using a weighted-decay structure: 35% for the most recent year, followed by 25%, 20%, 12%, and 8% for the preceding four years. This approach gives greater importance to current management while still recognizing the accumulated benefits of conservation investments made in previous years.

By combining predicted yield, climate indicators, and conservation-management history, the framework produces a final decision matrix that can help evaluate how conservation performance may be connected to potential payment outcomes. The goal is to provide an understandable and data-informed tool for exploring the relationship between agricultural productivity and sustained conservation practices.

The presentation received positive feedback from conference attendees. Several participants approached Dr. Fulton after the session to discuss the model and its outputs. Attendees highlighted the value of applying artificial intelligence to agricultural conservation and expressed particular interest in the direct connection between conservation payments and crop-yield outcomes. The project's final decision matrix was also recognized as one of the strongest and most useful results of the work.

The presentation demonstrates how AI and data-driven agricultural models can move beyond prediction alone by translating complex environmental, management, and production data into practical decision-support information for researchers, conservation professionals, policymakers, and agricultural producers.

items.title: ICICLE Team Presents AI & Cyberinfrastructure at ExploreAg Technology Camp
items.description: SAI Lab / ICICLE members presented AI and cyberinfrastructure tools to high school students at ExploreAg — Ag Technology Camp, with hands-on demos of Smart Labeling, Segmentation, and Intelligent Edge Management services.
items.author: NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
Institute team members Brijesh Nanda B Y, Harikesh Byrandurga Gopinath, Qifeng Chen, Aswathnarayan Radhakrishnan and Neelima Savardekar had the privilege of presenting at the ExploreAg - Ag Technology Camp in Columbus, Ohio and represent NSF ICICLE AI Institute.

Discussed how cutting-edge technology—from precision data to automation—is actively changing the way we grow, harvest, and sustain our food supply. This was an excellent opportunity for the high school students to get their hands on ICICLE's AI & CI Service pipeline using Smart Labeling Service, Segmentation Service & Intelligent Edge Management Service to process images.

Talked all things ag tech, explored real-world applications, and looked at where the industry is heading next. Incredible energy from the students exploring how tech and STEM drive modern farming.

A huge thank you to the ExploreAg team at Ohio Farm Bureau, Ohio State University College of Food, Agricultural, and Environmental Sciences (CFAES Food, Agricultural and Biological Engineering Department) for hosting such a high-impact experience for the high school students as they look at various career pathways related to food and agriculture in Ohio.

items.title: ICICLE Webinar: AI in Agriculture
items.description: The NSF-funded ICICLE AI Institute hosted a webinar highlighting how artificial intelligence supports scalable, data-driven decision-making across modern agricultural systems.
items.author: NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
On February 27, 2026, the NSF-funded ICICLE AI Institute hosted the webinar “AI in Agriculture,” highlighting how artificial intelligence is supporting scalable, data-driven decision-making across modern agricultural systems.

The webinar showcased ICICLE’s Data-to-Action (DTA) pipeline, which supports end-to-end workflows that integrate data ingestion, model training, inference, and interactive decision support. Demonstrations included a Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot for querying agricultural datasets and ICICLE resources, real-time object detection and classification pipelines for identifying crop health conditions and field objects, and a precision spot-spraying application for site-specific weed management.

Together, these demonstrations illustrated ICICLE’s efforts to make agricultural AI more accessible, interoperable, and impactful. The webinar also emphasized the importance of collaboration among computer scientists, agricultural engineers, researchers, and other domain stakeholders in advancing sustainable farming technologies.

The full webinar recording is available on YouTube.

items.title: NSF ICICLE Webinar: AI-enabled Digital Agriculture — An Overview of ICICLE Software Components
items.description: A webinar covering ICICLE's software components including HARVEST, Open Pass & ArrayMorph, demonstrating how AI-enabled tools are advancing digital agriculture research and practice.
items.author: NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
NSF ICICLE faculty member Hari Subramoni delivered a webinar for the NSF ICICLE AI Institute titled AI-enabled Digital Agriculture - An Overview of ICICLE Software Components. The session presented ICICLE’s work in developing low-cost, open-access, and intelligent cyberinfrastructure powered by high-performance computing and artificial intelligence for agriculture.

During the presentation, Hari introduced ICICLE’s end-to-end digital agriculture pipeline, enabling farmers to tailor unique solutions for their farms through the pipeline. He highlighted key software components specifically designed by ICICLE:

  • Harvest: The primary deep learning framework that manages the model training pipeline, semi-supervised image labeling, distributed HPC inference, and visualization dashboard through an easy to use interface.
  • ArrayMorph: A data transfer optimization tool that crops high-resolution satellite/aerial images down to just the target area before transferring, speeding up data transfer by ~1.5x and reducing cloud transfer costs by ~9x.
  • OpenPass: An automated drone navigation and data acquisition software that manages autonomous waypoint planning, field-level image capture, edge data streaming, and optional on-device edge processing.

Together, these technologies support the broader mission of democratizing AI, bringing high-performance computing and intelligent cyberinfrastructure directly to agricultural communities.

items.title: Hari Subramoni Presents ICICLE Digital Agriculture and AI at the 7NRP Workshop
items.description: NSF ICICLE faculty member Hari Subramoni presented ICICLE's Digital Agriculture Pipeline, introduced the institute's AI and cyberinfrastructure research, and participated in a panel discussion on AI and robotics in agriculture at the Seventh National Research Platform Workshop.
items.author: NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
NSF ICICLE faculty member Hari Subramoni represented The Ohio State University and the NSF ICICLE AI Institute at the Seventh National Research Platform (7NRP) Workshop, held May 5–7, 2026, at the University of California San Diego in La Jolla, California.

On May 5, Hari led the tutorial Using ICICLE Digital Agriculture Pipeline. The session introduced ICICLE's end-to-end digital agriculture workflow, connecting field data collection and processing with artificial intelligence and high-performance computing resources.

On May 6, Hari delivered a presentation titled AI Institute. He introduced the mission of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and its work to develop accessible, reusable, and intelligent cyberinfrastructure across edge devices, cloud platforms, and high-performance computing systems.

Hari later joined Ryan Dinubilo of F3 Innovate and Konstantin Karydis of the University of California Riverside for a Panel Discussion on artificial intelligence in agriculture. The discussion followed presentations on agricultural AI, intelligent cyberinfrastructure, and mobile robots for automated field data collection and analysis.

Through the tutorial, presentation, and panel discussion, Hari highlighted how ICICLE connects foundational AI and cyberinfrastructure research with practical digital agriculture applications. The sessions demonstrated the importance of integrating field sensors, edge computing, AI models, robotics, data management, and shared computing resources into reliable end-to-end agricultural workflows.

View the complete 7NRP Workshop schedule, presentations, and recorded media.
